implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: validation returns std::vector<Error> (or appends to a caller-owned vector) instead of throwing; each check push_backs a small Error struct and the caller renders every entry. No new type is required - the vector plus a plain struct replaces the classic Notification class - and std::string_view keeps the entries cheap. Prefer this shape on C++17 toolchains; reach for std::expected when the caller should also receive the parsed value from the same object.
pitfalls: Returning by value is cheap with move semantics, but a const std::vector<Error>& out-parameter still spreads the validation idiom through every signature - pick one shape per codebase.
Deciding failure by errors.empty() is only sound if no check can throw behind your back (for example a std::stoi that throws); a stray exception bypasses the accumulator.

variants.name: std::expected carrying the error list (C++23)
variants.implementation_notes: std::expected (C++23) represents either the parsed value or the unexpected error side, so a validation either yields the constructed value or the complete list of Errors inside one value - no out-parameter and no exception. It is the analogue of Rust's Result and Haskell's Either, and monadic helpers (and_then, transform, or_else) let callers chain further steps; choose it when the toolchain is C++23 and the caller benefits from receiving value and errors through the same channel.
pitfalls: std::unexpected must wrap a value of the error type; constructing expected with the error list directly is a compile error, and .value() throws bad_expected_access - use the boolean test or value_or.
Monadic chains short-circuit: and_then on an expected that already holds errors skips the remaining steps, which is the fail-fast behaviour the accumulator was meant to avoid for independent checks.
